subject: science
passage: The juniper forest around Ziarat, in the dry mountains of Balochistan, Pakistan, is one of the largest of its kind in the world. The trees grow with extraordinary slowness: in the thin soil and sparse rainfall of the region, a juniper may add only a few centimeters of height in a year, and some of the oldest trees are thought to be well over a thousand years old. This slowness is also the forest's weakness. A tree cut for firewood or killed by drought cannot be replaced within a human lifetime, so losses that would be minor in a fast-growing forest can take centuries to repair at Ziarat.
stem: Based on the text, why is the loss of a tree at Ziarat a more serious problem than it would be in many other forests?

choices.A: The trees are so old that they no longer produce seeds.
choices.B: The forest contains fewer trees than any other juniper forest in the world.
choices.C: The thin soil of the region prevents any new seedlings from taking root.
choices.D: The trees grow so slowly that a replacement takes centuries to reach the same size.

explanation.why: The text explains that the junipers grow "with extraordinary slowness," and then calls this slowness "the forest's weakness": a lost tree "cannot be replaced within a human lifetime," so losses "can take centuries to repair." The seriousness of a loss comes from the slow growth.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text does not say the old trees stop producing seeds.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text calls the forest one of the largest of its kind, not one with the fewest trees.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the thin soil slows growth; it does not say seedlings cannot take root.
explanation.D: Correct. The text links the problem directly to the slow growth rate, which makes replacement take centuries.
